questions.question: Which of the following best describes the one circumstance in which encryption of message content is permitted in an amateur transmission?
options: Never — encryption is prohibited in all amateur transmissions without exception
When using a remote control link that operates in an amateur band above 30 MHz
When assisting a User Service that needs to protect a casualty's identity (licence condition 6-19)
When communicating with a station in a country that requires encrypted identification
questions.explanation: Licence condition 6-19 permits an encrypted message (or other method of obscuring meaning) specifically when assisting a User Service — such as mountain rescue or ambulance — where the identity of a casualty may need to be protected. The decision to encrypt rests with the User Service, not the amateur. In all other circumstances encryption is prohibited.

questions.question: Why are Q-codes and standard abbreviations (such as 73 or CQ) permitted in amateur transmissions even though the licence requires plain language?
options: They are classified as digital modes and therefore exempt from the plain language requirement
They are permitted only on CW (Morse code) transmissions — not on voice
They facilitate passing messages under poor conditions and do not obscure meaning in the way that encryption would
They are granted a specific exception under the Communications Act 2003
questions.explanation: Q-codes and standard abbreviations are permitted because they are widely understood by licensed amateurs and facilitate communication when conditions are difficult or language barriers exist. Crucially, they do not obscure the general meaning of a transmission the way encryption would — any properly trained amateur can decode them. The Wireless Telegraphy Act distinction is between obscuring meaning (forbidden) and aiding efficient communication (permitted).

questions.question: The Wireless Telegraphy (Content of Transmission) Regulations 1988 prohibit which category of amateur message?
options: Messages addressed to a specific named individual rather than a callsign
Messages about commercial activities, even when supporting a public event
Grossly offensive, indecent, or menacing messages
Messages sent during a contest that do not include the full station identification
questions.explanation: The WT (Content of Transmission) Regulations 1988 specifically prohibit grossly offensive, indecent, or menacing content. Commercial use restrictions arise from the licence conditions (6-4) rather than these Regulations. Breaching the WT Regulations could be grounds for licence revocation.

questions.question: The Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 defines 'Undue Interference' as:
options: Any interference that is noticed by a member of the public
Interference that affects a neighbouring property regardless of duration
Persistent and harmful interference to wireless telegraphy
Interference that results in a formal complaint to Ofcom
questions.explanation: The WT Act 2006 defines Undue Interference specifically as persistent AND harmful interference. A single brief episode of interference, or interference that causes no harm, does not meet the statutory definition. Your transmitter must be designed, maintained, and operated so it does not cause Undue Interference to any wireless telegraphy.

questions.question: Under licence condition 7-1, when may an Ofcom-authorised person inspect your amateur radio equipment?
options: Only after a formal written complaint has been received from a third party
Only if you have been operating outside the permitted frequency bands
Either if an urgent situation exists, or simply to verify that you are operating in accordance with your licence
Only during the annual licence renewal period
questions.explanation: Licence condition 7-1 gives an Ofcom-authorised person the right to inspect your station and equipment either if they believe an urgent situation exists (e.g. excessive field strengths causing EMC problems) OR simply to ensure you are operating in accordance with your licence. No prior complaint is required — it can be a routine compliance check.

questions.question: The Full licence requires you to conduct periodic tests on your transmissions. What is the primary purpose of this self-testing obligation?
options: To generate a log entry that satisfies Ofcom's annual reporting requirements
To satisfy yourself that your station is not causing Undue Interference and that transmissions are clean and stable
To verify that your power output matches the level declared on the licence application
To provide evidence for RSGB award applications
questions.explanation: The self-testing requirement (1D1) exists so that you can satisfy yourself — and demonstrate to Ofcom if required — that your station is operating correctly: frequency-stable, spectrally clean, and not causing Undue Interference. Keeping records of these tests is good practice and provides evidence of compliance if a neighbour complaint escalates.

questions.question: You want to control your amateur transmitter remotely using a radio link. The link frequency you have chosen is 144.500 MHz (in the amateur 2 m band). Is this permitted, and why?
options: No — all remote control links must use non-amateur frequencies
Yes — 144.500 MHz is above 30 MHz, which satisfies the requirement for amateur-band control links (condition 6-10b)
Yes — any frequency may be used for a remote control link provided it is in the amateur schedule
No — only internet-based links are permitted for remote control; radio links require a separate Ofcom licence
questions.explanation: Licence condition 6-10b specifies that if the control link uses an amateur band, it must operate above 30 MHz. 144.500 MHz satisfies this requirement. Links below 30 MHz in amateur bands are not permitted for remote control use. Internet links have no such frequency constraint.

questions.question: Your remotely operated station's internet control link fails unexpectedly. You cannot stop the transmission. Which licence condition has most directly been breached?
options: The transmitter must not operate above 100 W when unattended
The control link must be adequately secure and able to promptly turn off the transmitter — loss of the link must stop transmissions (fail-safe requirement)
All remote control must use amateur-band links above 30 MHz rather than internet protocols
You must be physically present within 50 km of the transmitter at all times during operation
questions.explanation: Conditions 6-10 and 6-10x require the control link to be adequately secure and able to promptly turn off the transmitter. Critically, the link must be fail-safe: if the link is lost, transmissions must stop. A remote station that continues transmitting after control link loss is not operating in accordance with the licence, regardless of the link technology used.

questions.question: When operating your amateur station remotely from a location other than your registered main station address, what must be displayed at the remote operating location?
options: A full copy of your amateur radio licence certificate
A notice displaying your Licence Number (condition 6-10d)
Your name and home address
The operating frequency and transmit power in use
questions.explanation: Licence condition 6-10d requires you to display a notice at the remote location giving your Licence Number. This allows anyone at that location to contact Ofcom if needed — only Ofcom can match the licence number to your personal details, protecting your privacy. You are not required to display your personal address.

questions.question: CEPT Recommendation T/R 61-01 permits operation in signatory countries without obtaining a local licence. Which UK licence holders may use this facility?
options: All UK amateur licence holders — Foundation, Intermediate, and Full
Foundation and Intermediate licence holders only, as Full licensees already hold an international HAREC
Full licence (HAREC) holders only — it does not extend to Foundation, Intermediate, club, or reciprocal licences
Any licensee who has passed a Morse examination at 12 words per minute
questions.explanation: T/R 61-01 explicitly applies only to holders of a personal Full licence, which carries the HAREC (Harmonised Amateur Radio Examination Certificate). It does not extend to Foundation or Intermediate licences, club station licences, or reciprocal licences. This is a common exam distinction — the HAREC is issued by the RSGB to all UK Full licence holders.

questions.question: Which organisation issues the HAREC certificate to successful UK Full licence candidates?
options: Ofcom, on completion of the Full licence examination
The ITU, as the international regulatory body
CEPT, as the originator of the T/R 61-01 recommendation
The RSGB, as the national amateur radio society
questions.explanation: The HAREC (Harmonised Amateur Radio Examination Certificate) is issued by the RSGB to all UK Full licence holders on passing the Full exam. Ofcom issues the licence itself; the RSGB issues the HAREC as the national amateur radio society. The ITU and CEPT set the framework but do not issue individual certificates.

questions.question: You are a UK Full licensee (call sign M0ABC) operating in France under CEPT T/R 61-01. Which call sign format is required?
options: M0ABC/F — your UK call sign followed by a stroke and the host country prefix
F/M0ABC — host country prefix, stroke, then your UK call sign
M0ABC/P — the standard portable designation used in the UK
FM0ABC — the two letters combined without a stroke
questions.explanation: T/R 61-01 requires the host country code to precede your home call sign, separated by a stroke: F/M0ABC for France. This identifies both which country you are operating from (F) and your home call sign (M0ABC). The UK portable convention (M0ABC/P) is not the CEPT international format.

questions.question: Under CEPT T/R 61-01, for what maximum period may a UK Full licensee operate in a signatory country without obtaining a local licence? And what must be done for a stay exceeding that period?
options: 6 weeks — after which a bilateral reciprocal licence must be arranged
6 months — after which you must apply to Ofcom for an extension
3 months — after which you may use the HAREC to apply for a local licence under T/R 61-02
1 year — after which you must sit the host country's amateur examination
questions.explanation: T/R 61-01 covers temporary non-resident operation for up to 3 months. For stays exceeding 3 months, T/R 61-02 (the HAREC framework) allows you to apply for a full licence in the host signatory country, recognised as equivalent to passing their own examination. You do not need to re-sit the local exam if your HAREC is accepted.

questions.question: The United Kingdom falls within which ITU Radio Region?
options: Region 2
Region 1
Region 3
Region 4
questions.explanation: The UK is in ITU Region 1, which covers Europe, Africa, Russia, the Middle East, and former Soviet republics. There are only three ITU regions — there is no Region 4.

questions.question: You hold a UK Full licence and are temporarily operating from a country in ITU Region 2 under a reciprocal agreement. The 17 m band (18 MHz) is listed in your UK licence schedule. Before transmitting on 18 MHz, what must you verify?
options: That 18 MHz is allocated to amateur radio in ITU Region 2 as well as in your UK schedule
That you have at least 6 months' experience on the 17 m band in the UK
That your HAREC certificate has been endorsed for HF operation
That you do not exceed 100 W on any HF frequency in Region 2
questions.explanation: ITU amateur allocations differ between regions. A frequency in your UK schedule (Region 1) may not be allocated to amateur radio in Region 2 (Americas). You must use only frequencies that appear in BOTH your UK licence schedule AND the regional amateur allocation for the country you are operating from. Using a Region 1 frequency that is not allocated in Region 2 would be a breach of both the local regulations and your UK licence.

questions.question: Which geographic area forms ITU Radio Region 3?
options: Europe, Africa, and the former Soviet Union
North America, Central America, and South America
Asia, Oceania, and the Pacific
The polar regions, international waters, and aircraft
questions.explanation: ITU Region 3 covers Asia and the Pacific — including China, Japan, India, South-East Asia, Australia, New Zealand, and the Pacific Island nations. Region 1 covers Europe, Africa, Russia, and the Middle East. Region 2 covers the Americas.

questions.question: Below what EIRP thresholds does a UK amateur station NOT require a formal EMF compliance assessment?
options: Below 25 W average EIRP over 6 minutes, OR below 250 W instantaneous peak
Below 10 W average EIRP over any 6-minute period, OR below 100 W instantaneous peak EIRP
Below 1 W average EIRP over 6 minutes, OR below 10 W instantaneous peak
Below 100 W average EIRP over 6 minutes, OR below 1 kW instantaneous peak
questions.explanation: If EIRP is below 10 W averaged over any 6-minute period OR the instantaneous peak EIRP is below 100 W, no formal EMF exclusion zone assessment is required. Above either threshold, an assessment using the Ofcom/RSGB spreadsheet is mandatory. Most Full licence stations will exceed the average threshold and must therefore assess compliance.

questions.question: The amateur licence requires EMF field strengths around your station not to exceed ICNIRP limits applicable to the general public (Condition 9-1). Which of the following correctly identifies who is included in 'the general public' for this purpose?
options: Only members of the public on land adjacent to your property boundary
Non-amateur neighbours, family members, guests, and anyone in areas accessible to them — including your own garden, neighbours' gardens, and nearby public areas
Only children under 16, since adults are assumed able to move away from RF sources
Only Ofcom inspection personnel and visitors to your shack
questions.explanation: The 'general public' for ICNIRP purposes includes non-amateur family members and guests, neighbours, and any person in an area accessible to them — which includes your own garden, back garden, neighbours' gardens, and nearby public roads and paths. Licensed amateurs are assumed knowledgeable enough to protect themselves; the protective requirement is for those who are not. The 'affected area' may extend well beyond your own property.

questions.question: What does the 'Compliance Distance' output from the Ofcom/RSGB EMF assessment spreadsheet represent?
options: The minimum distance you must sit from your transmitter when operating
The horizontal distance from the antenna to the nearest location where the general public must not be present during transmissions
The radius beyond which your signal is guaranteed to be below ICNIRP occupational exposure limits
The distance between antenna and ground at which feeder losses have reduced EIRP to the threshold level
questions.explanation: The Compliance Distance (also called the exclusion zone distance) is the horizontal distance from the antenna to the nearest point at which members of the general public must not be present while you are transmitting. If this distance extends beyond your property boundary, you must either reduce power/gain (reducing EIRP) or demonstrate that public access to that area can be controlled.

questions.question: You increase your directional antenna's gain from 6 dBi to 12 dBi while keeping transmit power constant at 100 W. What is the approximate effect on the EMF Compliance Distance in the main lobe direction?
options: No change — compliance distance depends only on transmitter output power, not antenna gain
The compliance distance approximately doubles
The compliance distance quadruples
The compliance distance decreases — a higher-gain beam concentrates power into a narrower angle, reducing exposure at ground level
questions.explanation: EIRP = power × gain. Increasing gain from 6 dBi to 12 dBi multiplies gain by a factor of 4, so EIRP increases by a factor of 4. The far-field compliance distance scales with the square root of EIRP (since field strength E ∝ √EIRP / distance). Therefore the compliance distance increases by √4 = 2, i.e. it approximately doubles. Higher antenna gain always increases the compliance distance in the main lobe — it does not reduce it.

questions.question: Under which precise circumstances does the amateur licence permit operation without complying with the ICNIRP EMF guidelines?
options: During any RAYNET exercise or emergency preparedness training event
When operating exclusively on VHF or UHF bands at less than 50 W
When necessarily located at the site of a genuine emergency and conducting communications essential to that emergency response
When the transmissions last less than 2 minutes in total in any 6-minute period
questions.explanation: The emergency exception is narrow: you must be necessarily located AT the site of the emergency, and the communications must be essential to the ongoing emergency response. Pre-planned exercises, training events, and preparedness activities at a distance from an actual emergency do NOT qualify. The exception exists because it may be physically impossible to maintain compliance distances in an active emergency scene.

questions.section_name: Licence Conditions — Schedule 1 and Operating Conditions
questions.question: A call sign beginning with the prefix M9 belongs to which UK amateur licence class?
options: Full licence — M9 is an older Full licence series
Intermediate licence — M8 and M9 are the current Intermediate series
Foundation licence — M3, M6, M7, and M9 are all Foundation prefixes
Club station — M9 indicates a club special event call sign
questions.explanation: The M8 and M9 series were introduced for Intermediate licences from 2023 onward, replacing the older 2E prefix series. Full licences use M0, M1, M5 (and older G-series). Foundation licences use M3, M6, M7. Knowing these prefix series is required at Full level (Schedule 1 and Condition 6-23).

questions.section_name: Licence Conditions — Schedule 1 and Operating Conditions
questions.question: Schedule note G I i limits operation on 5 MHz. You are transmitting at 100 W PEP into an antenna with a gain of 3 dBi. What is your EIRP, and are you within the 5 MHz schedule limit?
options: EIRP = 103 W — exceeds the 100 W PEP limit, not compliant
EIRP = 200 W — exactly at the 200 W EIRP limit; compliant but with no margin
EIRP = 300 W — exceeds the 200 W EIRP limit; not compliant
EIRP = 50 W — below any limit; compliant because the antenna is only 3 dBi
questions.explanation: 3 dBi gain is a power ratio of 2× (10^(3/10) ≈ 2). EIRP = 100 W × 2 = 200 W. Schedule note G I i sets a generic EIRP limit of 200 W at 5 MHz in addition to the 100 W PEP limit. At 100 W PEP and 3 dBi, EIRP is exactly 200 W — compliant, but at the limit. Any higher gain or power on 5 MHz would breach the schedule condition. [Verify against current Ofcom schedule before operating.]

questions.section_name: Licence Conditions — Schedule 1 and Operating Conditions
questions.question: The UK amateur schedule states that 1.81–1.83 MHz is 'Primary. Available on the basis of non-interference to other services outside the UK or Crown Dependencies.' What does this mean for your transmissions on this frequency?
options: You have Primary status and absolute priority over all other users on this frequency worldwide
You may only transmit on this frequency if no other UK amateur is already using it
You must give way to any service outside the UK or Crown Dependencies that is a Primary user on this frequency, even though you also have Primary status within the UK
You must not transmit on this frequency at all — it is reserved for non-UK services
questions.explanation: This note means you have Primary status within the UK and Crown Dependencies — but you must still give way to any Primary user of this frequency from outside those territories. In practice this means that if a non-UK Primary service is using 1.81–1.83 MHz, you must not cause them interference, and must QSY if they are affected. Primary status within the UK does not confer worldwide priority. The convention is to move frequency if you feel transmission should not be there.

questions.section_name: Licence Conditions — Schedule 1 and Operating Conditions
questions.question: You have been operating from a temporary location for 35 minutes. Applying all relevant Schedule conditions, which of the following correctly summarises your identification obligations during that period?
options: Give your callsign at the start and end of each contact only — no other identification requirement applies at a temporary location
Give your callsign every 15 minutes; no obligation to announce the temporary location unless specifically asked
Give your callsign every 15 minutes (and on joining/leaving nets), announce your temporary location every 30 minutes, and have a telephone available at the number registered with Ofcom
Give your callsign every 5 minutes and transmit your location on 145.500 MHz FM as a safety announcement before each session
questions.explanation: From a temporary location, three distinct obligations apply simultaneously: (1) Schedule note G VI — identify with your callsign every 15 minutes and when joining/leaving nets; (2) Schedule note G VIII — give the temporary location every 30 minutes; (3) Schedule note G IX — you must have a telephone available at the number registered with Ofcom, so you can be reached immediately. After 35 minutes you should have given your callsign at the 15-minute mark, and the location at some point within the first 30 minutes.
